source.author: stat
source.text: sic ubi forte viris longum super aequor ituris, cum iam ad vela noti et scisso redit ancora fundo, haeret amica manus: certant innectere collo brachia, manantesque oculos hinc oscula turbant, hinc magni caligo maris, tandemque relicti stant in rupe tamen; fugientia carbasa visu dulce sequi, patriosque dolent crebrescere ventos.
source.text_original: sic ubi forte viris longum super aequor ituris, / cum iam ad vela noti et scisso redit ancora fundo, / haeret amica manus: certant innectere collo / brachia, manantesque oculos hinc oscula turbant, / hinc magni caligo maris, tandemque relicti / stant in rupe tamen; fugientia carbasa visu / dulce sequi, patriosque dolent crebrescere ventos.
source.text_english: Thus, when by chance for men about to travel long over the sea, when now the anchor, ready for the familiar sails and torn from the seabed, is being drawn up again, a loving hand clings on: they vie to wind their arms around the neck, and streaming eyes are troubled by kisses from this side, from that by the darkness of the great sea, and at last, though left behind, they still stand on the cliff; it is sweet to follow with the gaze the fleeing canvas, and they grieve to hear the home winds rise again and again.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: fervere cuncta virum coetu, simul undique cernit delatum nemus et docta resonare bipenni litora; iam pinus gracili dissolvere lamna Thespiaden iungique latus lentoque sequaces molliri videt igne trabes, remisque paratis Pallada velifero quaerentem bracchia malo.
reuse.text_original: fervere cuncta virum coetu, simul undique cernit / delatum nemus et docta resonare bipenni / litora; iam pinus gracili dissolvere lamna / Thespiaden iungique latus lentoque sequaces / molliri videt igne trabes, remisque paratis / Pallada velifero quaerentem bracchia malo.
reuse.text_english: he sees all things seething with a company of men, and at the same time the grove brought in from every side and the shores echoing with the skilled double axe; already the pine is being split into thin planks, the Thespian joined, and the sides fitted together, and the following timbers softened by the slow fire, and Pallas, with the oars prepared, seeking the arms on the sail-bearing mast.
